days.title: Carbohydrates
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure of carbohydrates.
  • Differentiate monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.
  • Explain the functions of carbohydrates.
  • Identify food sources.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Monosaccharide — single sugar unit (glucose, fructose).
  • Disaccharide — two sugar units (sucrose, lactose).
  • Polysaccharide — many sugar units (starch, glycogen, cellulose).
  • Glycosidic bond — bond between sugar units.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Structure

Carbohydrates contain C, H, O in a 1:2:1 ratio (CH₂O)ₙ. They are the body's primary quick-energy source.

B. Types

TypeExampleFunction
MonosaccharideGlucose, fructoseImmediate energy
DisaccharideSucrose, lactoseTransport sugar
PolysaccharideStarch (plants), glycogen (animals), cellulose (cell walls)Storage & structure

C. Functions in Metabolism

  • Primary source of ATP via cellular respiration
  • Structural component (cellulose in plant cell walls)
  • Energy storage (glycogen in liver and muscle)

💬 Let's Discuss

This week begins the study of biomolecules, the four big families of molecules that make up living things: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Three of them are polymers — long chains built from repeating units called monomers, the way a necklace is built from beads. Monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis (a water molecule is removed) and broken apart by hydrolysis (water is added back). Digestion is basically hydrolysis.

Carbohydrates contain C, H and O, usually in a 1:2:1 ratio (glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆). Their monomers are monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose (fruit sugar) and galactose. Two monosaccharides make a disaccharide: sucrose (table sugar = glucose + fructose), lactose (milk sugar) and maltose. Many make a polysaccharide.

Polysaccharides show how small changes in linkage create very different functions. Starch (in rice, corn, cassava) and glycogen (in our liver and muscles) are both glucose chains used to store energy; glycogen is more highly branched, so enzymes can release glucose from many ends at once during exercise. Cellulose is also made of glucose, but its bonds form straight, tough fibers for plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest cellulose, yet it is important as dietary fiber. Chitin, in insect shells and fungal walls, is a related structural polysaccharide.

Carbohydrates are the body's main source of quick energy: glucose is broken down in cellular respiration to make ATP. Common mistake: thinking glucose itself is the cell's energy currency. Glucose is the fuel; ATP is the currency the cell actually spends.

pairs.why: A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit such as glucose.
A disaccharide has two sugar units, like sucrose (glucose + fructose).
A polysaccharide is a long chain of many sugar units.
Glycogen is the branched storage form of glucose in animals.
Cellulose fibers form strong plant cell walls.
Starch is how plants store glucose.

scenarios.explanation: Glucose is a single sugar — a monosaccharide.
Sucrose is two sugars joined — a disaccharide.
Starch is a long chain of glucose — a polysaccharide.

scenarios.text: Which is found in plant cell walls?
scenarios.explanation: Cellulose makes up plant cell walls.

scenarios.text: Which is the body's stored form of glucose in animals?
scenarios.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen in liver and muscle.

scenarios.text: Primary function of carbohydrates in metabolism:
scenarios.explanation: Carbohydrates are broken down quickly to supply energy.

questions.text: What is the chemical ratio of C:H:O in carbohydrates?
questions.explanation: The general formula (CH₂O)n gives a C:H:O ratio of 1:2:1.

questions.text: Which polysaccharide is found in plant cell walls?
questions.explanation: Cellulose forms the plant cell wall; starch and glycogen store energy.

questions.text: Which carbohydrate is the main fuel that cells break down to make ATP?
questions.explanation: Glucose is the main fuel that cells break down to make ATP.

takeaways: Carbohydrates contain C, H, O in a 1:2:1 ratio.
Primary function is quick energy; also structural (cellulose) and storage (glycogen).
Glucose is the key energy molecule in cells.

days.title: Lipids
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure of lipids.
  • Differentiate triglycerides, phospholipids, and steroids.
  • Explain the functions of lipids.
  • Relate lipid structure to function.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Lipid — hydrophobic biological molecule.
  • Triglyceride — glycerol + 3 fatty acids (fat/oil).
  • Phospholipid — glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate group.
  • Steroid — four fused rings (e.g., cholesterol, testosterone).

📚 Lesson Content

A. Types of Lipids

TypeStructureFunction
TriglycerideGlycerol + 3 fatty acidsEnergy storage, insulation
PhospholipidGlycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphateCell membranes
SteroidFour fused ringsHormones, cholesterol

B. Saturated vs Unsaturated Fats

  • Saturated — no double bonds; solid at room temperature (butter)
  • Unsaturated — one or more double bonds; liquid at room temperature (olive oil)

C. Functions in Metabolism

  • Long-term energy storage
  • Structural component of membranes
  • Hormone synthesis (steroids)
  • Thermal insulation

💬 Let's Discuss

Lipids are a varied group that share one property: they are mostly hydrophobic, because they are made largely of long hydrocarbon (C–H) chains that do not mix with water. Unlike the other biomolecules, lipids are not true polymers.

Triglycerides (fats and oils) are made of one glycerol plus three fatty acids. Gram for gram, they store more than twice the energy of carbohydrates (about 9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g), so they are the body's long-term energy store. Fat under the skin also insulates the body and cushions organs. The shape of the fatty acid matters. Saturated fatty acids have only single bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and they are solid at room temperature — butter, lard, the fat in pork. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds that put kinks in the chain, so they cannot pack tightly and stay liquid — olive, canola and fish oils. (Coconut oil is an exception: plant-based but mostly saturated.)

Phospholipids replace one fatty acid with a phosphate group, giving a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails — the perfect shape for building membranes. Steroids have a skeleton of four fused carbon rings. Cholesterol is a steroid that keeps membranes fluid and is the raw material for hormones such as estrogen and testosterone and for vitamin D. Waxes waterproof leaves and feathers.

Common mistake: "All fat is bad." Lipids are essential for membranes, hormones and absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K. The concern is too much saturated and trans fat, which is linked to clogged arteries.

pairs.why: A triglyceride is one glycerol bonded to three fatty acids.
A phospholipid has two fatty acids and a phosphate group on glycerol.
Steroids have four fused carbon rings.
Straight saturated chains pack tightly, so the fat is solid.
Kinked unsaturated chains cannot pack tightly, so the fat is liquid.
Cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity and is used to make steroid hormones.

scenarios.explanation: A triglyceride is glycerol + 3 fatty acids.
Phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes.
Cholesterol has the four-ring structure of a steroid.
Butter is solid at room temperature — saturated fat.

scenarios.text: Olive oil is an example of:
scenarios.explanation: Olive oil is liquid at room temperature — unsaturated fat.
Stored fat gives long-term energy and insulation.

questions.explanation: Long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains make lipids hydrophobic.

questions.text: Which lipid type is a component of cell membranes?
Which of the following is NOT a function of lipids?
questions.explanation: Genetic information is stored in nucleic acids, not lipids.

takeaways: Three main types: triglycerides, phospholipids, steroids.
Functions: energy storage, membranes, hormones, insulation.
Saturated fats are solid; unsaturated fats are liquid at room temperature.

days.title: Proteins
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure of proteins.
  • Explain the four levels of protein structure.
  • List the functions of proteins.
  • Relate protein structure to function.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Amino acid — the monomer of proteins.
  • Peptide bond — bond between amino acids.
  • Denaturation — loss of protein shape/function.
  • Primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary — four levels of protein structure.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Amino Acids

20 different amino acids. Each has an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), and a variable R group.

B. Levels of Protein Structure

LevelDescription
PrimarySequence of amino acids
SecondaryAlpha helix or beta sheet (H-bonds)
Tertiary3D folding of the whole chain
QuaternaryMultiple chains (e.g., hemoglobin)

C. Functions of Proteins

  • Enzymes (catalysts)
  • Structural (collagen, keratin)
  • Transport (hemoglobin)
  • Signaling (hormones like insulin)
  • Defense (antibodies)
  • Movement (actin, myosin)

💬 Let's Discuss

If carbohydrates are fuel and lipids are storage, proteins are the workers of the cell. They speed up reactions (enzymes), carry substances (hemoglobin carries O₂), defend the body (antibodies), send signals (insulin), give structure (collagen, keratin) and make movement possible (actin and myosin).

The monomer of a protein is the amino acid. Each has an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain called the R group. There are 20 standard amino acids, and their R groups differ — some are polar, some nonpolar, some charged. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide chain.

A protein's job depends on its exact shape, which forms in four levels. The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, like letters in a sentence. The secondary structure is local coiling or folding — the alpha helix and beta pleated sheet — held by hydrogen bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall 3D shape of one chain, formed when R groups interact. The quaternary structure exists only when two or more chains join, like the four subunits of hemoglobin.

Changing one letter can change the meaning: in sickle-cell disease, a single amino acid swap in hemoglobin changes the protein's shape and makes red blood cells sickle-shaped. Heat, strong acids or bases, and salts can break the bonds that hold the shape. This is denaturation. When you fry an egg, the clear albumin turns white and solid because its proteins unfold and clump.

Common mistake: thinking denaturation breaks peptide bonds. It usually leaves the sequence intact but destroys the folded shape — and with it, the function.

pairs.why: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
A peptide bond links one amino acid to the next.
Primary structure is the order of amino acids.
Secondary structure is the local alpha helix or beta sheet.
Tertiary structure is the full 3D folding of one chain.
Quaternary structure is two or more chains joined together.
Denaturation unfolds the protein so it can no longer work.

scenarios.explanation: Amino acids are the monomers of proteins.

scenarios.text: An alpha helix is part of which level?
scenarios.explanation: Alpha helices are secondary structure.

scenarios.text: The amino acid sequence is which level?
scenarios.explanation: The sequence of amino acids is primary structure.
Four subunits joined together is quaternary structure.

scenarios.text: Cooking an egg denatures its proteins because:

choices.label: Water is added to the egg

scenarios.explanation: Heat breaks the bonds holding the protein's shape, so it denatures.
Antibodies are proteins that recognize and fight pathogens.

questions.text: How many standard amino acids are there?

questions.explanation: Denaturation is the loss of a protein's shape and therefore its function.

questions.text: Which is NOT a function of proteins?
questions.explanation: Genetic information is stored in nucleic acids, not proteins.

takeaways: Proteins are polymers of amino acids.
Four levels: primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary.
Functions: enzymes, structure, transport, signaling, defense, movement.

days.title: Nucleic Acids & Roles in Metabolism
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure of nucleic acids.
  • Differentiate DNA from RNA.
  • Explain the roles of biological molecules in metabolism.
  • Summarize the four biomolecules.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Nucleotide — monomer of nucleic acids (sugar + phosphate + base).
  • DNA — deoxyribonucleic acid; stores genetic info.
  • RNA — ribonucleic acid; transmits genetic info.
  • ATP — energy currency of the cell.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Nucleotide Structure

Each nucleotide has: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.

B. DNA vs RNA

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
StrandsDouble helixSingle strand
BasesA, T, G, CA, U, G, C
FunctionGenetic storageProtein synthesis

C. Roles in Metabolism

  • Carbohydrates: quick energy (ATP)
  • Lipids: long-term energy & membranes
  • Proteins: enzymes catalyze reactions
  • Nucleic acids: store and transmit genetic info

💬 Let's Discuss

Nucleic acids store and use genetic information. Their monomers are nucleotides, and each nucleotide has three parts: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar of one nucleotide bonds to the phosphate of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone with the bases sticking out.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) has the sugar deoxyribose and the bases A, T, G and C. It is a double helix: two strands held together by base pairs (A–T, G–C). DNA is the permanent "master copy" of instructions kept in the nucleus. RNA (ribonucleic acid) has the sugar ribose, uses uracil (U) instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. RNA is the working copy: mRNA carries the message to ribosomes, tRNA brings amino acids, and rRNA forms part of ribosomes.

One modified nucleotide, ATP (adenosine triphosphate), is the cell's energy currency. Breaking off its last phosphate releases energy that powers muscle contraction, active transport and building molecules.

Now put the four biomolecules together in metabolism: carbohydrates give quick energy; lipids give long-term energy storage, insulation and membranes; proteins act as enzymes that catalyze nearly every reaction; and nucleic acids store and express the information to make those proteins. A good example is a long run: you first burn glucose and glycogen, then increasingly rely on fat, while enzymes control every step.

Common mistake: "RNA has thymine." RNA has uracil; DNA has thymine.

pairs.why: Nucleotides are the monomers of DNA and RNA.
DNA is the stable, long-term store of genetic information.
RNA carries and uses the information to make proteins.
DNA's sugar lacks one oxygen — deoxyribose.
RNA's sugar is ribose.
Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.
Thymine is found only in DNA.
ATP releases energy when its last phosphate is removed.

scenarios.explanation: Carbohydrates are broken down quickly for energy.
Lipids store energy for the long term.
Enzymes, which are proteins, catalyze reactions.
DNA stores genetic information.

scenarios.text: Carries genetic info from DNA to ribosomes.
scenarios.explanation: mRNA carries the code from DNA to ribosomes.

scenarios.text: Primary energy currency of the cell.
scenarios.explanation: ATP is the energy currency spent by cells.

questions.text: What are the three components of a nucleotide?
questions.explanation: A nucleotide has a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.

questions.text: Which base is found in RNA but not DNA?
questions.explanation: Uracil is found in RNA in place of thymine.
Enzymes are proteins that catalyze metabolic reactions.

takeaways: Nucleotides are the monomers of nucleic acids.
DNA stores genetic info; RNA transmits it.
Each biomolecule plays a unique role in metabolism.
ATP is the energy currency produced from carbohydrates and lipids.
